Timely payment of goods and services will enhance liquidity and increase economic activity in the country. To ensure comprehensive reporting on budget performance, Accounting Officers should submit complete financial and non-financial reports on budget performance on time, including those of their SAGAs as per Section 83 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 and as per the guidelines issued from time to time by the Controller of Budget.

[1  INTRODUCTION]

The OCoB is established under Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya. Its primary mandate is to oversee the implementation of the budgets of the National and County Governments by authorizing withdrawals from public funds under Articles 204, 206, and 207 of the Constitution and to report on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. This report fulfils the requirements of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, by presenting progress on the budget implementation by the National Government in the first nine months of the FY 2021/22.

The report is presented in six chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two summarises receipts into the Consolidated Fund and exchequer issues to fund both National and County governments from the Consolidated Fund as approved by the Controller of Budget. Chapter three presents the overall budget performance in the first nine months of FY 2021/22, including expenditure disaggregated into significant budget items for ministerial development and recurrent budget. It also provides Consolidated Fund Services performance comprising of Public debt, Pension and gratuities, Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders, and pending bills status for the national government as of 31st March 2022.

Chapter four presents the financial and programme performance of the sixty-seven (67) MDAs, which are grouped under ten sectors aligned to MDAs' functions. Budget performance includes exchequer issues to net estimates and actual expenditure to gross estimates presented as a percentage of the annual estimates (absorption rate). The gross estimate is the printed allocations to the MDAs, which includes funding by the Government and external resources, which may be in the form of Appropriations-in-Aid (A-I-A) or revenue either as a loan or grant. Net estimates present financing by the government through the national exchequer.

[2.5.4 Exchequer Issues Under Article 223]

Article 223 of the Constitution allows the MDAs to access additional funding during the budget implementation process. Nonetheless, Article 223 (5) limits this access to ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that financial year unless in exceptional circumstances where Parliament has approved a higher percentage.

During the reporting period, the total exchequer request under Article 223 amounted to Khs.44.0 billion, or 1.4 per cent of the gross budget estimates, comprising Ksh.19.34 for recurrent and Kshs.24.66 billion for development expenditure.

Clause 2 of Article 223 requires the approval of Parliament for any spending under this Article to be sought within two months after the first withdrawal of the money, subject to clause 3. If Parliament is not sitting or adjourns before the approval, the approval shall be sought within two weeks in the next sitting. The first request under Article 223 was made on 30th August 2021, and Supplementary Budget I was approved at the end of March 2022, therefore, meaning that the requests for withdrawal under Article 223 made from August 2021 to January 2022 were not approved by Parliament within the timeline anticipated under Clause 2 of Article 223 of the Constitution.

The SPCR sector undertakes the promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, a productive workforce and gender equity and equality. Other key roles include empowering communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights, and promoting diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.

[4.11.2 Budget Performance for SPCR Sector]

The budgetary allocation to the SPCR sector in the FY 2021/22 amounts to Kshs.72.19 billion, representing 2 per cent of the gross national budget, compared to Kshs.59.95 billion allocated in the FY 2020/21. The allocation comprised Kshs.32.56 billion (45 per cent), for development activities and Kshs.39.64 billion (55 per cent), for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Social Protection, Pensions & Senior Citizens Affairs and Special Programmes received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.33.57 billion (46.5 per cent of the sector's budget). In comparison, the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.2.99 billion (4 per cent of the sector's funding).

Figure 4.19 shows the budgetary allocation trend for the SPCR sector for FY 2017/18 to FY 2021/22. Growth in budget allocation to the Social Protection, Culture and Recreation sector compared to FY 2020/21 is attributed to additional funding to cover new beneficiaries under the cash transfer programme under the State Department for Social Protection, Pensions and Senior Citizens Affairs and provision for the construction of stadia by the State Department for Sports. Significant allocations include; Kshs.16.7 billion for Cash Transfer to Elderly persons, Kshs.7.9 billion for Orphans and Vulnerable Children, Kshs.4.1 billion for Hunger Safety Net Programme and Kshs.1.2 billion for Cash Transfer to Persons with Severe disability.

[5.1 Introduction]

This chapter highlights the critical issues that affected budget implementation in the first nine months of FY 2021/22. Further, it provides recommendations to achieve effective budget execution by the government.

[5.2 Key Issues and Recommendations]

In overseeing budget implementation in the first nine months of the FY 2021/22, the Controller of Budget identified critical issues as discussed hereunder;

[5.2.1 High level of Exchequer Requests Under Article 223 of the Constitution]

Requests for withdrawal of funds under Article 223 of the Constitution were significantly high and, in some instances, related to activities that could have been provided as part of the regular budget estimates. Article 223 (5) limits the national government expenditure to ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that financial year unless in exceptional circumstances where Parliament has approved a higher percentage.

The analysis of exchequer issues under Article 223, releases to the following MDAs exceed the 10 per cent ceiling - Recurrent exchequer issues for the Ministry of Petroleum and Mining at 911.2 per cent. Others were; the Development exchequer for the following MDAs; Ministry of Defence - 19.7 per cent, the State Department for Early Learning & Basic Education at 24.6 per cent, the National Treasury at 16.7 per cent, the State Department for Infrastructure at 12.2 per cent, the State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research at 11 per cent and the State Department for Wildlife at 15.1 per cent.

Further, the State Department of Implementation of Curriculum Reforms did not have any provision in the original Budget as it was created after the conclusion of the budget process for FY 2021/22. Through the National Treasury, the State Department made exchequer requests totalling Kshs.22.4 million under Article 223 of the Constitution.

The Controller of Budget recommends strict adherence to the law in accessing and utilizing funds under Article 223 provisions of the Constitution.

[5.2.2 High Level of Public Debt]

As of 31st March 2022, public debt stock stood at Kshs.8.40 trillion, recording a 14.6 per cent growth from Kshs.7.34 trillion reported as of 31st March 2021. From the analysis of public debt growth, the exchange rate may be a contributing factor to this growth, given that 49.9 per cent of the public debt is denominated in foreign currency. The exchange rate of the Kenya Shilling to the US Dollar at the beginning of the financial year in July 2021 averaged at Kenya shillings 108.04 to the US dollar compared to the exchange rate as of 31st March 2022, when the dollar averaged 114.61 per Kenyan shilling, a difference of 6.57 Kenya shillings (6.08 per cent exchange rate depreciation). The depreciation of the Kenya shilling causes an increase in the stock of public debt in Kenya shilling terms and an increase in the debt cost (principal and interest). A growing foreign currency-denominated public debt in the background of a depreciating shilling necessitates an increase in the amount required for debt repayment provided for in the budget.

The Controller of Budget recommends that the National Government considers debt restructuring, hedging strategies, and the mopping up of idle cash held by public institutions. There is need to ensure borrowing is at a minimal cost and effective exchange rate control to reduce the high expenditure on payment of both principle and interest amount since most foreign debt is denominated in US dollars.

[5.2.3 Low Absorption of Development Budget]

As of 31st March 2022, the overall budget absorption level stood at 61.1 per cent against a prorated expectation of 75 per cent at the end of the first nine months of the FY 2021/22. This aggregate absorption comprised 47.5 per cent and 64.6 per cent for development and recurrent budgets, respectively. The absorption of the development budget was far below the target.

To ensure timely implementation of development activities, the Controller of Budget recommends that Accounting Officers expedite procurement processes to ensure programmes are executed in line with work plans. The timely implementation of programs will also enable payment before the end of the financial year and avoid accumulating pending bills.

[5.2.4 Accumulation of Pending Bills]

Accumulated pending bills figures reported from the Quarterly Economic and Budgetary Review Report published by the National Treasury shows that the total outstanding national government pending bills as of 31st March 2022 amounted to Kshs.434.5 billion, comprising Kshs.385.6 billion (88.7 per cent) for State Corporations and Kshs.48.9 billion (11.3 per cent) for MDAs respectively.

The Controller of Budget recommends that all MDAs and State Corporations ensure payment of the eligible pending bills is guided by the National Treasury Circular No.7/2019, which states that pending bills be prioritised as a first charge in the subsequent cycle of budget implementation, which most MDAs seem not to comply with National Treasury Circular No.7/2019.

[5.2.5 Delay in Submission of Financial and Non-financial Reports to the Controller oBudget]

The Controller of Budget is required under Article 228(6) of the Constitution to submit a budget implementation report for national and county governments to Parliament every quarter. The CoB provided guidelines and formats to MDAs to guide them when submitting their financial and non-financial reports for the first nine months of the FY 2021/2022 in to enhance uniformity and compliance in reporting.

However, some MDAs did not submit their reports as per the guidelines issued and did not disclose some expenditures and submitted latter than expected date. Non-disclosure of budget performance information may result in under-reporting and not reflecting the actual position of budget performance.

The Controller of Budget therefore, recommends that all Accounting Officers ensure that financial and nonfinancial performance reports reflect the proper position of the budget performance for accurate reporting and on timely manner as per Section 83 (4) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012.
